newsitem.title: USA: Dlr ends up in U.S., shakes off Hashimoto remarks.
newsitem.headline: Dlr ends up in U.S., shakes off Hashimoto remarks.

text.p: The dollar edged higher along with U.S. stocks and bonds in relief after Japanese officials downplayed fears sparked on Monday that Japan would pare its massive holdings of U.S. government securities.

On Monday, Japan's Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto fuelled a huge drop in the Dow Jones industrials and pushed the dollar and U.S. Treasuries lower by saying Japan had in the past been tempted to sell its Treasury holdings due to the volatility in foreign exchange rates.

"It would be both a short-term and a long-term negative if those events came to pass, but obviously I don't think anybody seriously thinks the Japanese are going to declare that type of economic retaliation on us," said Elliott Dix, an assistant vice-president and trader at Signet Bank in Richmond.
"People have basically discounted it at this point," he added.

The Ministry of Finance said on Tuesday that Japan would continue to cooperate with the United States to stabilize exchange rates and Hashimoto regretted that his intentions had not been accurately portrayed.
Hashimoto spoke in Japanese to a group of investors at Columbia University in New York and some confusion surrounded the accuracy of the English-language translation of his remarks.
The damage control by Japanese officials prompted a jump in the Dow, which unofficially closed up 154 points at 7758, compensating for Monday's near 200-point plunge.

The dollar gained to 114.90/95 yen from 114.65/75 at the open and to 1.7240/50 marks from 1.7235/45. Traders said the dollar faces tough resistance above 115 yen, where offers from Japanese trust banks lurk.

The market was focused on tonight's expected release of the Bank of Japan's quarterly tankan survey of corporate sentiment, seen as an important clue to the central bank's monetary policy. The survey is set for release at 2350 GMT.
It is expected to show weak business sentiment. The key manufacturers' index for the second quarter was forcast at -0.8 against a 2.0 reading previously.

"Everyone is waiting for this number out of Japan. If it is -2.0 or less, people will buy dollars on that and we would break 115 yen," said Doug Lee, an assistant vice president and trader at Sakura Bank Ltd in New York.
Stealing the spotlight was the pound, which fell from a 59-month peak of 2.8818 marks after a Goldman Sachs & Co research report said sterling was overvalued by 15 percent.

"There are some comments out about sterling being overvalued that caused sterling/mark to come down a big figure and cable to move down below $1.6650," said Mark Gargano, head of currency derivatives at First Union National Bank.
The Goldman report, The Weekly Analyst, was also skeptical that sterling would rise to 3.0 marks, as some market players had forecast.

Cable drifted below support at $1.6650/60 but partially recovered by the close to end at $1.6690/00 compared to $1.6697/04 at the open. Sterling/mark fell to 2.8743/53 by the close from 2.8788 at the open.
The dollar received a small lift after the Conference Board said U.S. consumer confidence reached a 28-year high in June, with its index reading 129.6 compared to a revised 127.9 in May.
Also bolstering the dollar was San Francisco Federal Reserve Bank President Robert Parry who said he sees no clear sign of an end to the U.S. economic recovery which is currently in its seventh year.
Parry added he sees robust U.S. growth and well-behaved inflation and that, despite Hashimoto's remarks, there should be no significant drop in overall demand for U.S. securities.
In other trading, the dollar fell to 1.4380/90 Swiss francs from 1.4385/90 and gained to Canadian $1.3905/10 from C$1.3882/87. The Australian dollar closed lower at $0.7500/05 from $0.7506/11.
((-- Roanne Daniels, 212-859-1677))
